title: AI in Search
hook: Search engines now answer in sentences, not just links. Convenient — but the AI summary can be wrong or miss context, and the links underneath are still where the truth lives.
key_points: AI 'overviews' summarize the web for you instead of just listing pages.
Faster for simple questions; riskier for anything important or contested.
The summary can be confidently wrong or strip away crucial context.
Treat it as a starting point — click through to the real sources to confirm.
content_html: Search has quietly changed. Type a question into Google or Bing and you increasingly get an AI-written summary at the top — an "overview" or "AI answer" — instead of just a list of blue links. For a simple, low-stakes question ("how many tablespoons in a cup?") this is genuinely convenient: you get the answer without clicking. But it's worth understanding what changed, because the trade-off is real.
extra_html: These summaries are generated by the same kind of language model behind chatbots, which means they inherit the same flaws. They can be confidently wrong, blend sources into a misleading statement, or strip out the context that made the original answer correct — all while sitting at the very top of the page in an authoritative-looking box. Early versions produced some now-famous absurd answers, and subtler errors are harder to catch. The healthy habit is the same one for chatbots: treat the AI summary as a quick starting point, not the verdict. For anything that matters — health, money, a decision, a contested fact — scroll past the summary and click into the actual sources underneath, where you can see who's saying it and judge for yourself.

related.title: When AI Makes Things Up
related.hook: AI 'hallucinations' aren't glitches — they're the technology working as designed. A model that always predicts a plausible next word will sometimes produce a plausible falsehood.

related.title: How to Fact-Check AI
related.hook: You can't tell a true AI answer from a made-up one by reading it — both sound equally sure. So build a habit: for anything that matters, verify it somewhere that isn't the AI.

related.title: Chatbots & Assistants
related.hook: ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini feel like talking to a person, but they're generative AI with a chat wrapper — brilliant writing partners, unreliable encyclopedias.

related.title: A Court Just Pushed Back on AI Search
related.hook: A German court ruled against Google's AI Overviews — the AI summaries atop search results — in a decision that could reshape AI search and back publishers who don't want their work summarized away.

related.title: Meta's New AI Search Answers From Facebook Posts
related.hook: Meta added an 'AI Mode' to Facebook search that builds answers out of public posts. Convenient in theory — but early hands-on testing found it confidently getting things wrong.

choices.text: It can be confidently wrong or drop important context

flashcards.explanation_html: The summary is generated, so it inherits AI's flaws — it can be inaccurate or oversimplified, while looking authoritative at the top of the page.

flashcards.prompt: How should you treat an AI search summary?
flashcards.back_html: As a starting point, not the final answer — click through to the actual sources to confirm anything that matters.
